Encapsulation adds layer-specific headers and sometimes trailers as data moves down the protocol stack.
The Application layer supplies network services closest to user applications.
DNS resolves names to records including IPv4 A and IPv6 AAAA addresses.
FTP is specifically designed for file transfer between clients and servers, although ordinary FTP does not encrypt credentials or content.
The Presentation layer conceptually handles representation, translation, compression, and encryption.
MAC addressing belongs to local-link delivery at the Data Link layer rather than data representation at the Presentation layer.
The Session layer conceptually establishes, manages, synchronizes, and terminates application dialogues.
Half-duplex communication supports both directions but only one at a time; full duplex permits simultaneous transmission.

The Transport layer can provide reliable end-to-end delivery, sequencing, and flow control, as TCP does. Not every transport protocol offers these guarantees.
A TCP transport PDU is called a segment; network packets and link frames are different encapsulation levels.
UDP sends connectionless datagrams without built-in delivery, ordering, or retransmission guarantees, reducing transport overhead for suitable applications.
Transport ports distinguish application endpoints and enable multiplexing and demultiplexing traffic.
The Network layer handles logical addressing and routing between networks.
A router selects next hops using Layer 3 routing information; ordinary switches and bridges primarily forward link-layer frames.
ICMP carries IP control/error messages and supports Echo Request/Reply used by ping.
The Network layer uses logical addresses such as IPv4 and IPv6; MAC addresses identify link-layer endpoints.
The Data Link layer frames traffic for a local link and can detect errors; Ethernet error detection does not itself guarantee retransmission or reliable delivery.
The IEEE 802 architecture distinguishes Logical Link Control and Media Access Control sublayers.
The link-layer PDU is a frame, containing a payload and link-specific control information.
An Ethernet frame's FCS contains a CRC used to detect many transmission errors; detection is distinct from correction or retransmission.
The Physical layer encodes and transmits bit signals over the medium.
A hub repeats physical signals to the other ports without learning MAC addresses or routing IP packets.
The conventional Ethernet MAC address is 48 bits, usually displayed as six hexadecimal octets. Other identifier formats also exist.
For a universally administered EUI-48 address, the traditional 24-bit OUI identifies the assigned organization, usually the manufacturer.
ARP resolves an on-link IPv4 address to a link-layer address. IPv6 uses Neighbor Discovery instead.
The conventional TCP/IP reference model has four layers; a common teaching variation separates the link layer into two and uses five.
TCP/IP combines the OSI upper three layers into its Application layer.
SYN, SYN-ACK, and ACK establish a TCP connection and synchronize sequence numbers before ordinary data exchange.
TCP provides an ordered reliable byte stream through sequencing, acknowledgments, and retransmission; an unrecoverable connection failure is reported rather than an absolute promise of delivery.
The Internet layer uses IP addressing and routing to carry packets between networks.
Flow control protects receiver buffers using the advertised receive window; congestion control is the separate mechanism that responds to network congestion.
IPv4 is an Internet-layer protocol. TCP is transport, HTTP application, and Ethernet link/network-interface technology.
MAC addresses identify local-link interfaces and IP addresses provide logical routing identity. MAC addresses can be locally changed or randomized, so permanence is not guaranteed.
SSH provides encrypted remote login and management at the Application layer.
Sequence numbers and acknowledgments let TCP track received byte ranges, restore ordering, and retransmit missing data.
Network-layer traffic is encapsulated in packets; link traffic uses frames and the Physical layer carries bits.
A damaged fiber affects the physical transmission medium and is a Layer 1 fault.
The TCP/IP Network Interface layer handles link framing and the medium-specific delivery mechanisms associated with Ethernet or Wi-Fi.
